title: What does the SOCI Act require for critical infrastructure personnel?
description: How the SOCI Act CIRMP Rules treat critical workers, AusCheck background checks and insider risk for energy assets, and where training fits after June 2026.
shortAnswer: The Security of Critical Infrastructure Act 2018 requires responsible entities for specified assets, including critical electricity, gas, liquid fuel and energy market operator assets, to keep a critical infrastructure risk management program. Section 9 of the CIRMP Rules requires them to identify critical workers, allow access to critical components only after a suitability assessment, and minimize risks from malicious or negligent staff and off-boarding. The Rules prescribe no training course, so training is a control the program must justify.
keyTakeaways: The CIRMP Rules (LIN 23/006) commenced on February 17, 2023. Compilation No. 2 at June 10, 2026 incorporates the Enhanced Critical Infrastructure Risk Management Program Rules 2026, which commenced that day.

Baseline section 9 requires a process to identify critical workers, assess their suitability before access to critical components, and minimize risks from malicious or negligent employees and contractors and from off-boarding.

Enhanced section 9A applies to critical electricity, gas, liquid fuel and energy market operator assets, among others. It requires an AusCheck background check or a Negative Vetting 1 or higher clearance, rechecks at least every 5 years, and ongoing monitoring of suitability.

Section 8 requires compliance with a named cyber framework, such as the AESCSF at Security Profile 1 or the Essential Eight at maturity level one, within 12 months after the applicable period. Enhanced section 8A raises this to Security Profile 2 or maturity level two.

The CIRMP Rules do not use the word training. Awareness and training obligations reach critical workers indirectly, through the program's duty to minimize negligent insider risk and through the chosen cyber framework.
regulator: Cyber and Infrastructure Security Centre (CISC), Department of Home Affairs
appliesTo: Responsible entities for critical electricity, gas, liquid fuel and energy market operator assets

sections.heading: What is a CIRMP and which energy assets need one?

blocks.text: A critical infrastructure risk management program (CIRMP) is the written program Part 2A of the Security of Critical Infrastructure Act 2018 requires a responsible entity to adopt and maintain for each specified asset. The [CIRMP Rules](https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2023L00112/latest/text), made under section 61 of the Act, specify which assets are covered and what the program must contain for each hazard type: cyber and information security, personnel, supply chain, and physical security and natural hazards.

Section 4(1) lists the covered assets. For the energy sector they are critical electricity assets, critical energy market operator assets, critical gas assets and critical liquid fuel assets. Section 4A(1) then places all four of those energy classes, plus broadcasting, domain name systems, freight and water, in the group subject to enhanced requirements added in 2026.

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects Compilation No. 2 of the Security of Critical Infrastructure (Critical infrastructure risk management program) Rules (LIN 23/006) 2023, compiled at June 10, 2026, as at November 2026. The enhanced requirements commenced on June 10, 2026 with grace periods of 12 and 24 months under section 4A(6). Confirm how those periods apply to a specific asset with the Cyber and Infrastructure Security Centre or legal advisers.

sections.heading: What does section 9 require for personnel hazards?

blocks.text: Section 9 requires the CIRMP to contain a process or system to do three things: identify the entity's critical workers; permit a critical worker access to critical components of the asset only where the worker has been assessed as suitable; and, as far as reasonably practicable, minimize or eliminate material risks arising from malicious or negligent employees or contractors and from the off-boarding of outgoing employees and contractors.

The Rules define a personnel hazard as including a critical worker acting, through malice or negligence, to compromise the proper function of the asset or cause significant damage to it. Negligence is the part of that definition that training addresses. A background check can screen out a person with relevant criminal history, but it cannot stop a well-intentioned operator from approving a remote access request they should have refused.

At baseline, section 9(2) says the suitability assessment may be an AusCheck background check, and a note confirms that entities outside the enhanced group are not required to use AusCheck. Section 9(6) requires the entity to have regard to whether the CIRMP lists its critical workers and describes the personnel risks that could have a relevant impact on the asset.

sections.heading: What extra personnel controls apply to energy assets from June 2026?

blocks.text: Section 9A, added by the Enhanced CIRMP Rules 2026, applies to assets listed in section 4A(1), which includes every energy class. It tightens the suitability test and adds access management duties.

items: **Suitability, section 9A(4):** a critical worker may be assessed as suitable only after an AusCheck background check followed by the entity's own assessment, or if the worker holds a relevant security clearance, defined as an active clearance at Negative Vetting 1 level or higher.
**Recheck interval, section 9A(5)(c):** where ongoing access is required, the AusCheck background check must be repeated at least every 5 years.
**Ongoing monitoring, section 9A(3)(b):** the program must proactively monitor, identify and act on developments that may affect a critical worker's ongoing suitability.

**Access management, section 9A(2):** the program must minimize or eliminate risks from unauthorized or unsupervised access to critical components, compromise or misuse of credentials and privileged access, access by people who are not critical workers, and incoming and outgoing critical workers.
**Exceptions, section 9A(3)(a)(ii):** if a critical worker cannot meet the suitability test, the CIRMP must record the risk and the actions taken to minimize it.

blocks.text: Section 4A(6) gives a 12 month grace period for the section 9A(2) access management duties and a 24 month grace period for the rest of section 9A. Programs that rely on training to reduce credential misuse or unsupervised access should plan that training within the shorter window.

sections.heading: How do the cyber framework requirements bring in awareness training?

blocks.text: Section 8 requires each responsible entity, within 12 months after the applicable period, to maintain a process to comply with one of five named frameworks or an equivalent: AS ISO/IEC 27001:2015, the Australian Signals Directorate's Essential Eight at maturity level one, the NIST Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity, the US Department of Energy's Cybersecurity Capability Maturity Model at Maturity Indicator Level 1, or the 2020-21 AESCSF Framework Core published by the Australian Energy Market Operator at Security Profile 1.

For enhanced assets, section 8A raises the bar to AS ISO/IEC 27001:2023, Essential Eight maturity level two, NIST CSF 2.0, the Cybersecurity Capability Maturity Model version 2.1 at Maturity Indicator Level 2, or the 2023 AESCSF Framework Core at Security Profile 2. Whatever training these frameworks expect becomes part of the CIRMP once the entity adopts one. An entity choosing ISO/IEC 27001, for example, takes on its competence and awareness clauses, described on the [ISO 27001 awareness training](/regulations/iso-27001-awareness-training-requirements) page.

sections.heading: Does the SOCI Act require critical workers to be trained?

blocks.text: Not directly. The CIRMP Rules contain no clause that names a course, a frequency or a training topic. What they require is a program that minimizes material risks from negligent insiders, controls credential misuse and privileged access, and manages onboarding and off-boarding. Training is one of the controls an entity can use to meet those duties, and if the CIRMP relies on it, the training becomes something the entity must be able to evidence.

That makes the design question different from prescriptive regimes such as [NERC CIP-004 training](/regulations/nerc-cip-004-training-requirements), which fixes quarterly awareness and a 15 calendar month training cycle. Under SOCI, the entity sets the content and frequency by reference to its own risk assessment and chosen framework, and must be ready to explain why that is enough. The guide on [mapping training to compliance obligations](/guides/how-to-map-training-to-compliance-obligations) describes a method for that justification.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry records each CIRMP personnel risk as a node linked to the critical worker roles it affects and to the controls chosen for it, including any training and its assessment points. When the Rules or the program change, the roles whose training relies on the changed control can be identified from those links rather than by reviewing every course.

faqs.q: Who counts as a critical worker?
faqs.a: The term is defined in the Act, as a note to section 3 of the CIRMP Rules confirms, and the Rules build on it by requiring each entity to identify its critical workers and list them in the program. The list should cover the people whose malice or negligence could compromise the asset's function or cause significant damage, because that is how the Rules define a personnel hazard.

faqs.q: Is an AusCheck background check mandatory?
faqs.a: For assets in the enhanced group in section 4A(1), including critical electricity, gas, liquid fuel and energy market operator assets, section 9A(4) requires an AusCheck check followed by a suitability assessment, unless the worker holds a Negative Vetting 1 or higher clearance. For other assets, section 9(2) makes AusCheck one permitted option rather than a requirement.

faqs.q: How often must critical workers be rechecked?
faqs.a: For enhanced assets, section 9A(5)(c) requires the AusCheck background check to be repeated at least every 5 years for a person requiring ongoing access to critical components. Where suitability rests on a security clearance, section 9A(6) requires revalidation or an AusCheck check before the clearance lapses. The program must also monitor suitability between checks.

faqs.q: Does the SOCI Act set a frequency for security awareness training?
faqs.a: No. The CIRMP Rules do not set any training frequency. If an entity relies on awareness training to minimize negligent insider risk or credential misuse, it should set and document a frequency in its program by reference to its risk assessment and to the cyber framework it has adopted under section 8 or 8A.

factCheck.claim: The CIRMP Rules were registered on February 16, 2023 and commenced on February 17, 2023; Compilation No. 2 at June 10, 2026 includes F2026L00701, registered June 9, 2026 and commenced June 10, 2026
Section 4(1) lists critical electricity, energy market operator, gas and liquid fuel assets among covered assets; section 4A(1) places them in the enhanced requirements group

Section 9(1) requires a process to identify critical workers, permit access to critical components only after a suitability assessment, and minimize risks from malicious or negligent employees or contractors and from off-boarding; section 9(2) allows AusCheck

Section 9A(4) requires an AusCheck background check and assessment or a relevant security clearance (Negative Vetting 1 or higher); section 9A(5)(c) requires rechecks at least every 5 years for ongoing access

Section 8(3) and (4) require compliance within 12 months after the applicable period with a listed framework, including the 2020-21 AESCSF at Security Profile 1 and Essential Eight maturity level one; section 8A lists enhanced frameworks including Security Profile 2 and maturity level two
Section 4A(6) sets a 12 month grace period for sections 6A, 8A(2) and 9A(2) and a 24 month grace period for the remaining enhanced provisions
The amending instrument is titled Security of Critical Infrastructure Legislation Amendment (Enhanced Critical Infrastructure Risk Management Program) Rules 2026
